div.p: T h e development of control-dominated embedded systems can be largely automated by making use of formal models of computation. I n some of these models functional objects are not independently activated, triggered by time or external events, as in conventional real-time scheduling models, but each communication between any two functional objects carries a n activation signal f r o m the sender to the receiver. This paper presents a n application of scheduling theory to reactive real-time transactions (task groups) implementing a formal model of this kind, used in the context of the P O L I S toolset: a network of extended Finite State Machines communicating asynchronously. Task instances are activated in response t o internal and/or external events and the objective of the scheduling problem is to avoid the loss of events exchanged by the tasks and to minimize the number of task instances activated in response t o external events. T h e paper presents a schedulability analysis, two priority assignm e n t algorithms, and a n experimental part with a dashboard controller example.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: This paper presents results in developing and then applying an innovative real-time scheduling theory to reactive embedded control systems implementing a network of extended Finite State Machines communicating asynchronously.

Formal models have been used for more than one decade for the description of the functional properties of embedded control systems (hardware and software). Most of these systems have a reactive, event-driven behavior and realtime constraints in terms of responsiveness to the external events. In order to provide sound real-time analysis to these systems it is of great importance to analyze the formal models on which the existing commercial CASE tools are based .

Most commercial toolsets decouple the functional computation from the interprocess communication. One such example is the Objectime toolset based on the ROOM methodology [lo]. In ROOM, the (real-time) system is designed from the composition of active objects (actors) and the reactive behavior is modeled using finite state machines (FSM). If all FSMs are activated synchronously, conventional Rate Monotonic analysis [8] can be applied to the design [9]. In other cases, such as the one presented here and based on another CASE tool, the POLIS toolset, a different event-based activation model is assumed. The analysis of the corresponding real-time scheduling problem reveals a non-conventional task activation model that probably needs further investigation from the real-time research community. The algorithms and results presented in this paper also apply to other models with a similar task activation semantics where each software component is implemented a s a port automaton, such as the one implemented in the VCC (Virtual Component CO-design) toolset by Cadence.

The scheduling theory discussed in the paper targets reactive (or event-based) systems where all tasks are executed on a single processor. Tasks represent finite-state objects that are executed asynchronously in response to external or internal(activati0n) events and communicate through the production and consumption of events. Furthermore, they do not have explicit deadlines (at least not in the traditional form). Rate constraints (a minimum inter-arrival time) apply to external events. The scheduling problem consists of making sure that no critical event (internal or external) is ever dropped by the system, that is, every critical event is always consumed before another event of the same kind is produced again.

The optimal solution to this scheduling problem can be found in exponential time [3]. In this paper, we are interested in some worst-case (pessimistic) analysis that can be run quickly and still overcome some of the problems found in earlier solutions. In this paper we also show how our scheduling theory may be applied to a real-world application: a dashboard controller example.

2 Overview of the POLIS model P O L I S [5] is a codesign environment targeted toward realtime reactive embedded system. Implementations of these systems are usually composed of software on a microcontroller and semi-custom hardware components like FPGAs.
Central to POLIS is a uniform behavior representation for hardware and software modules called Codesign Finite State Machines (CFSMs).

After the design is described, based on estimates of the implementation costs as hardware or software, it is partitioned into cooperating hardware and software modules. Hardware and software are then automatically generated for a given partition. In the case of hardware synthesis, the resulting circuit is then implemented and optimized using standard hardware synthesis techniques, [ll].

In the case of software synthesis, a CFSM is first translated into a control/data-flow diagram (called an s-graph, tions for software graph). The s-graph has a direct representation in C and can be translated with equal ease into object code by any available compiler.

To implement a valid behavior of a network of CFSMs, additional code is needed to perform the following funcschedule individual CFSMs implemented in software (sw-CFSMs) such that each one is executed in a timely manner , provide a mechanism for event emission and detection between sw-CFSMs, provide a mechanism for transferring events between CFSMs implemented in hardware and those implemented in software, This code is synthesized automatically. It is called RTOS, because it performs communication and scheduling functions traditionally performed by an operation system. The choice of scheduling policy, as well as the priority assignment in case of static priority scheduling is left to the user. In this paper we show how these choices can be automated.

div.head: CFSMs
div.p: A CFSM, like a "standard Finite State Machine (FSM), transforms a set of inputs into a set of outputs with only a finite amount of internal state. The difference between the two models is that the "standard definition of concurrent FSMs implies that all the FSMs change state exactly at the same time. On the other hand, a software implementation of a set of FSMs generally interleaves them in time. Hence the synchrony hypothesis is replaced in POLIS by a finite, non-zero reaction time.

The basic observable entities that define system behavior are events. An event is identified by a n a m e , a value from a finite set (e.g., {ON, OFF}), and a t i m e of occurrence. Some events, such as the user hitting the "reset" button, may not have an "interesting" value.

A CFSM consists of sets of input and output event names and a transition relation: a finite set of cause-reaction pairs, where each cause is a set of events names and values and each reaction is a set of output events and values. Each transition is triggered by the input events and emits, after a non-zero time, the output events. Once a CFSM is implemented, the actual worst case computation delay can be determined (e.g. by simulation) and used to verify time-dependent properties of the system. The state of the CFSM consists of those event names that are both the input and output for it.
The transitions of each CFSM are "atomic"; all output events of a given transition must be emitted before the next transition can occur.

The CFSM definition can be made to fit into a tasking model where a transaction represents a collection of tasks connected by an activatiori graph. Each CFSM corresponds to a task and the network of CFSMs corresponds to a set of transactions, a transaction being a set of related tasks.

Each task in a transaction can be activated by external or internal events. Tasks produce events at the completion of their execution and consume all the incoming events that are active at the time they start running. External events are constrained by a minimum inter-arrival time. Each internal event is sent on a single position buffer. If a n event is overwritten by U new one, i t is said to be "dropped". It is very common t o implicitly assume there is enough buffer space to hold all events and signals exchanged by tasks or to assume that each buffer has an associated resource handler. Both assumptions are wrong in the context of embedded systems. the range of 0 r.p.m. to 8000 r.p.m.

In [2], where this problem was discussed first (in the context of design automation) the proposed solution focuses on internal buffering: priorities are assigned trying to prevent the loss of internal events. Only in a second time the possible loss of external events (to which interarrival constraints apply) is considered. As a result, priorities are assigned on the basis of the task relationships and not on timing constraints (external events having the highest rate are the most likely to be lost). A second possible disadvantage is the execution of multiple instances of the same task in response to a single external event. This additional load can prove extremely undesirable when multiple transactions are active in the system.

The example shown in figure 4, which is a simplified version of a shock absorber controller [2], shows how tasks can he activated multiple times by external events. Tasks are shown as circles. The numbers inside the circles are the worst case execution times. The numbers between parenthesis are the priorities. If priorities are assigned as proposed in [2] (top graph, priorities prevent the loss of inter-nal events), the scheduling sequence is 15 time units long, including three instances of task 74. If priorities are assigned as shown in the lower half (tasks producing events always have prjorities higher than tasks consuming them), the schedule length reduces to only 8 time units and each task is executed just oncc The second priority assignment minimizes the computation produced in response to external events, but if the arrival pattern were the one on the lower right half, the scheduling would not be feasible (event e(3,4) is dropped). In this case priorities must be assigned in order to satisfy necessary conditions for guaranteeing some of the internal events.

A more recent work [3] from the same author presents a new priority assignmen.t scheme that avoids most of the undesirable (multiple) task executions. The algorithm (described in section 6) is proven to produce an optimal solution in a subspace of all possible priority assignments. Unfortunately, there is nl3 guarantee that a better solution does not exist outside th.e selected subspace. This limitation could be awn acceptable compromise in order to obtain a simpler (although pessimistic) procedure for predicting the schedulability of all events. In this paper we further improve this result by 0 formalizi.ng the necessary conditions for guaranteeing internal events that can he activated by more than one external event or can be activated multiple times by a single task; 0 providing a general procedure for computing the load generated by the execution of any task (internal or external) ; 0 providing both an optimal and an approximate priority assignment algc'rithms. The approximate solution allows to minimize the number of required priority levels.

Solving the schedulirig problem requires understanding the conditions for guaranteeing the internal events and finding a procedure that assigns priorities to tasks. Once this framework is in place, the worst-case real-time analysis we apply is a busy-period analysis ([12] [13] and many others).

Step b, which is crucial for the good functioning of the algorithm, has been described in the previous section. Its objective is to find a set of tasks generating the events on a suitable cut. Since there are many possible cuts we need some way to choose one of them. One possibility is to perform the changes for every possible cut and pick the one that results in the lowest margin left for guaranteeing the external events. When it is impossible to perform an exhaustive search (because of the large number of possible cuts) an heuristic should be chosen. For example, it could be possible to select the cut spanning the lowest number of events (which is an instance of a bipartite graph matching problem.) The first step consists in finding the events E,, that cannot be guaranteed (Theorem : 2 and Theorem 3) and making them safe by finding a suitable cut in the event graph and lowering the priority of the tasks generating events on the cut.

If T' = {rf,rg,. . . , r;2} is the set of tasks generating the events on the cut, then each task 7 , ' must have a priority lower than the priority of those tasks {rti, r i i , . . . ,T:~} consuming the events in .En9 generated because of its execution. Given a cut, the proposition leaves a (possibly large) number of legal priority assignments. An adaptation of Audsley's algorithm can be used to choose a (unique) priority level for all tasks, and this assignment is optimal with respect to the given cut [l]. In Audsley's algorithm all tasks start at the highest possible priority level and priorities are assigned sequentially, starting from the lowest. Each priority level is tentatively assigned to a task. If the task set can be scheduled, than the priority level is assigned to the task, and the algorithm continues. If no task can be found, then the task set is not schedulable. In fact, if no task can be scheduled with the current priority level, neither it would be scheduled with one of the already assigned (lower) priority levels.

In our case the priority levels are constrained, so there is only a limited subset of tasks from which to choose the one to be assigned the current (lowest) priority level. First, we build a graph G containing an arc from task ~i to task r1 if 7, must have a lower priority than rj . Arcs in G represent the priority constraints.

At this point, as in Audsley's algorithm, we assign all tasks the highest possible priority levels allowed by the priority constraints specified in 1. Then, priorities are assigned sequentially, starting from the lowest. The algorithm works iteratively: on each step only those tasks that have no incoming links are eligible for scheduling. We select one of those tasks and tentatively assign it the lowest available priority level. If all events received by the selected task are found to be schedulable (by using the procedure described in Section 7), the task is assigned its priority and removed from G together with its outgoing arcs, meaning that the precedence constraints on its priority level do no longer hold (all priority levels assignedby the algorithm from now on will be higher). If the task is not found schedulable another eligible task is tried. If all tasks can be successfully assigned a priority, the set is found to be schedulable.
The most serious problem with this solution is the need for a (possibly) large number of different priority levels, since each task must be assigned a unique priority.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: We implemented the two algorithms shown in the paper and we tried them on a number of task sets with different statistics: Our load-generating program produced sample transactions with the following parameters (All uniform distributions except for the rate that is fixed.) I parameter I values J min-max number of tasks per transaction min-max number of external tasks per transaction min-max number of events per task Inin-max number of events per external task rat,e of external events 8 t o 2 2 1 to 10 400 units 0.1 to 1.0 minimum utilization of processor

The minimum utilization has been computed as the ratio of the sum of the computation times of all tasks divided by the period of activation of the external tasks. Since tasks can be activated by more than one external task and more than once in response t o an external event (Theorem 4) the utilization shown in the graphs is an underestimate of the actual one.

On our test computer (a 350MHz Pentium I1 class PC) the number of tasks was practically limited to be less than 30 if an exhaustive search on all possible cuts had to be performed on a large number of task sets. The average running times for evaluating transactions of different size is shown in Figure 10. Please note, the figure only gives a rough idea of the required computation times (in seconds), and for a selected configuration (1.5 average incoming events per task for the first set, 1.75 for the second set). The variance in the execution times is expected to be very large. Beyond 30 tasks, the algorithm can still be run, provided the graph analysis shows a limited number of possible cuts. If this is not the case, a limitation on the number of cuts to be evaluated is necessary.

The outcome of the experiments is the percentage of schedulable transactions. The first experiments have been performed on task sets of limited size (9 and 12 total tasks), a short number of external tasks (2) and 1 to 2 events generated by each task (internal or external). The rate of the external events is initially constant. The results (on 5000 sample sets per point) are represented in figure 11. It is important to point out how there is no significant difference (less than lop3 in the percentage of schedulable sets) in the performance of the two algorithms. The two algorithms perform almost identically in every set where the activation rate of the external events is the same. Figure 11 shows the result of the first simulation batch (the percentage of sets found schedulable is actually a function of many different parameters.) The results for task sets of respectively 14 and 18 tasks, when the number of external tasks is 40% of the number of total tasks and the number of outgoing links was limited to 1 for the external tasks confirms that the two algorithms perform almost identically.

It is necessary to have at least two different rates (minimum interarrival times) for the external events t o appre-Figure 11: Schedulable ratio vs. utilization. 9 and 12 tasks per transaction, limited priority set (first algorithm) ciate the difference between the two algorithms. Figure 12 shows the fraction of schedulable transactions for 12 total and 4 external tasks per transaction. The difference between the two algorithms now results in 10% more sets found schedulable by the optimal algorithm in a wide range of utilizations. Increasing the number of external rates apparently does not widen nor restrict the performance gap between the two algorithms. In order to validate the proposed algorithm, we tried it on two task graphs, corresponding to the design of our dashboard controller and the design of a shock absorber controller. The first sample task set was tested using our algorithm. Not surprisingly, one single graph cut needed to be examined, and the set was found schedulable.

div.head: UllP
div.p: The second, more complex (and more realistic) task set we tried is the result of the design of a shock absorber system. It consists of 54 tasks, 8 of which are external. The set was tested for schedulability. Even though it consists of 54 tasks, the algorithm found one single cut. The schedulability analysis, taking into account the only possible cut, revealed the set to be non-feasible. In this case it was not immediate to find the bottlenecks, since many events failed at once the schedulability test. The first outcome of the guarantee results was to try reducing the execution time of all tasks in the same proportion (which could roughly correspond to the use of faster hardware than our 4MHz 68HCll controller) to see what reduction was necessary if all events had to be guaranteed given the original minimum interarrival rates of the exi,ernal tasks. In this case we found all computation times had to be reduced by a factor 8.5 to get a schedulable set. Tht: problem in this case is the large difference betwleen minimum (or average) and maximum computation times. In fact, the algorithm found a feasible priority assignment when the minimum computation times were considered. One possible solution, in this case, could be to split the load and/or use a faster processor.

div.head: Future Work
div.p: It is possible to improve the pessimism of our schedulability analysis procedure by considering the following: 0 the behavior of some (if not many) CFSMs depends on a counter: the w'xst case execution time happens only when the counter reaches a pre-defined trigger value, say k, that is at most once every k executions.

0 Our activation graph model assumes that each CFSM fires all output events in response to any possible combination of input e\.ents. in reality the semantics of the CFSM determines which output events (not all)
are produced.

While it is possible to improve our busy period analysis including a better model for the worst case computation time, the second problem is much more complicated and requires an entirely new way of modeling CFSMs semantics and their interactions. g-abstractions, proposed in [4] can be a suitable model, although, at this time, it is not clear how to use them in the context of real-time schedulability analysis.

div.head: Concliusions
div.p: In this paper: we presented an iterative solution to the scheduling problem in reactive real-time systems represented by a network of asynchronously communicating FSMs. We developed a priority assignment scheme and a tight worst-case analysis. All results are rigorously derived. We described application of tbe method to a dashboard controller example. Further experimental results are offered to exemplify the procedure a.nd its quality.
